plannerPlan.title: Starlight Festival on Nova Station
plannerPlan.contentScopeRationale: The worksheet is one coherent band: equal-groups multiplication and its division inverse within single-digit factors (products to 48, plus a 36-light array task). Items 1, 5, and 6 ask the learner to recognize an equal-groups structure inside a story; items 3 and 2 require the inverse (missing factor, sharing 40 into 5 equal rows); items 4 and 8 require the array model and commutativity/factor-pair flexibility; item 7 requires derived-fact reasoning from a near neighbor rather than recall alone. The smallest coherent program therefore centers on one construct — equal-groups/array structure and its factor-product-quotient relationships — rather than fact drill. Facts-to-48 recall is treated as a supporting prerequisite, not the target, because every item that needs a fact also needs the learner to decide which fact applies. Scope excludes multi-digit multiplication, remainders, and two-step operations beyond the single repeated-group step in item 5, since nothing on the page probes them. The chart shows a Grade 4 learner working on a Grade 3 page with no recorded math accuracy, so the charter must be diagnostic across the whole band instead of assuming a narrow gap.

concept.name: Equal-Groups and Array Structure with Factor-Product Relationships
concept.statement: A multiplication situation is a count of equal groups: the number of groups times the size of each group gives the total, the same total can be modeled as a rectangular array whose rows and columns are the two factors, and division is the inverse question that recovers a missing factor from the total. Knowing this structure lets a learner map a story or array onto an equation, find a missing factor, generate factor pairs for a total, and derive an unknown fact from a nearby known one.
concept.instanceScope: Grade 3 festival-themed page, products and totals within 48: 7 groups of 6; 40 shared into 5 equal rows; missing factor in __ x 8 = 48; two equations for a 4-by-9 array; three groups of 8 taken twice; identifying which story matches 6 x 7 among equal-groups, additive, and sharing distractors; correcting 5 x 9 = 40 using a nearby fact; producing two different equal-row arrays totaling 36. Single-digit factors only; no remainders; no multi-digit computation.
prerequisites: Skip counting and repeated addition within 50
Reading and writing multiplication and division equations with a symbolic unknown
Recognizing rows and columns in a rectangular array
Recall or reliable derivation of multiplication facts with factors 2 through 9
assumptions: The page's binding difficulty is deciding which multiplicative structure a situation has (equal groups vs. inverse vs. additive), not retrieving the product once the structure is chosen.
The learner's fluency with multiplication facts through 9 x 9 is unknown and should be probed rather than assumed either way.

A Grade 4 learner assigned Grade 3 multiplication content is either reviewing foundations or has an unresolved gap in multiplicative structure, so content should be pitched at full Grade 3 depth without remedial pacing until evidence says otherwise.
Forward equal-groups problems (7 x 6) will be more secure than inverse ones (40 into 5 rows; __ x 8 = 48), because the inverse requires holding the total fixed while searching for a factor.

Generating multiple factor pairs for one total (two arrays for 36) and producing two equations for one array are the highest-demand items because they require treating a total as decomposable in more than one way.
A moderate attention span with mixed learning style supports a compact program that probes the full construct band once, rather than an extended sequence covering each item type separately.
No diagnoses, IEP, or documented support needs constrain how this content is presented, so academic demand can be set by the construct alone.

plannerPlan.academicTheory: This learner most likely holds multiplication as a procedure attached to a fact table rather than as a structure that can be read off a situation. The page is built to break that: item 6 offers an additive and a sharing distractor for the same numbers, item 5 hides a repeated group inside a two-step story, item 7 rewards deriving 45 from a neighbor fact instead of retrieving it, and items 4 and 8 demand that one total be seen as more than one rectangle. So the diagnostic question is not "can the learner multiply within 48" but "can the learner decide what kind of multiplicative question is being asked, and move flexibly between total, factors, and array." The theory is that performance will hold on forward equal-groups items and degrade on inverse and multi-representation items (ASM-04, ASM-05), with fact recall as a confounder that must be measured separately (ASM-02) so a structural error is never misread as a computation slip. Because the entire evidence base is empty — no math accuracy, no fact bank, no prior decisions, no support observations — the smallest coherent program must sample every face of the construct once (forward equal groups, inverse/missing factor, array-to-equations, factor-pair generation, structure discrimination, derived fact) at Grade 3 depth, so a single pass separates the recall hypothesis from the structure hypothesis. Confirmation looks like clean forward work with breakdown concentrated in inverse and factor-pair items; disconfirmation looks like uniform difficulty across all six faces, which would relocate the target to fact fluency and the prerequisite band, or uniform success, which would push the construct toward multi-digit and multi-step extensions above Grade 3.

boardWorld.title: Starlight Festival on Nova Station
boardWorld.narrative: Creator is the newly hired Festival Engineer aboard Nova Station, a space outpost where alien families are arriving for the once-a-year Starlight Festival. The station's power grid runs on equal groups: lantern racks, snack pods, badge crates, and light walls only switch on when their groups are counted and wired correctly. Every solved problem sends visible power down the station's glowing conduits, lighting up another district of the festival. The chapter opens in the Arrival Dock (three shared activities that restore basic power), then Creator chooses one of two festival wings to bring fully online — the Light Wall Wing, where power is arranged in glowing grids, or the Market Wing, where power flows through the stories of the stall-keepers. A final optional Repair Bay lets Creator fix miswired circuits other engineers got wrong. When a wing is complete, the festival launches: the whole station lights up and alien crowds pour in under a drone-lantern sky.
boardWorld.backgroundPrompt: Deep indigo space with a warm festival glow rising from the station: brass-and-teal station hull, strings of paper-lantern satellites, soft aurora ribbons behind the star field. The board map is the station seen from above, districts dark until powered, each completed activity flooding its district with warm amber light and tiny animated alien crowds. Conduit lines pulse gently between nodes to show the path. Palette: indigo/charcoal backgrounds, amber/gold progress light, teal UI accents. Nothing flashes rapidly; motion is slow drifting lanterns and a gentle station rotation.

learningResponsibilities.title: Discriminate multiplicative from additive and sharing structures
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Test the core misconception the page targets: treating the same two numbers as a sum or a share instead of a group-count, which is the error the multiple-choice item is designed to expose.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given several stories using the same pair of numbers, select the one that matches a given multiplication expression and justify why the others are not equal-groups situations.

learningResponsibilities.title: Recover a missing factor from a known total
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Probe the inverse direction predicted to be weaker than forward multiplication, covering both symbolic missing-factor equations and equal-sharing contexts as the same underlying move.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given a total and one factor — presented either as an equation with an unknown or as an equal-rows sharing story within 48 — determine the missing factor and name the multiplication fact that verifies it.

learningResponsibilities.title: Translate between arrays and equations
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Check that rows and columns are read as factors and that commutativity is understood as two descriptions of one array rather than two unrelated facts.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given a rectangular array, write both multiplication equations it represents and explain what the rows and columns each count.

learningResponsibilities.title: Generate multiple factor pairs for one total
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Probe the highest-demand face of the construct — treating a total as decomposable in more than one way — which distinguishes structural understanding from single-fact recall.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given a total with several factor pairs within single-digit factors, produce two distinct equal-row arrangements that use the whole total and record the equation for each.

learningResponsibilities.title: Derive an unknown fact from a nearby known fact
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Separate the recall hypothesis from the structure hypothesis by testing whether an incorrect product can be repaired through reasoning about groups rather than re-retrieval.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given an incorrect product for a single-digit fact, identify a neighboring fact, adjust by one group, and state the corrected product with the reasoning that fixes it.

learningResponsibilities.title: Handle a repeated equal-groups step inside a story
learningResponsibilities.purpose: Test whether equal-groups reasoning survives when the situation requires applying the structure twice, which is the only multi-step demand on the page.
learningResponsibilities.academicTarget: Given a story where equal groups each contribute a quantity on two occasions, compute the total and show the multiplicative structure used.

fork.question: After the Arrival Dock is powered (the three shared activities), the station map splits into two glowing wings. Creator taps one wing to fly a small maintenance pod toward it. Each wing shows a 5-second looping preview of its first activity's opening action — dragging lantern rows into a grid for the Light Wall Wing, or dealing flags into equal rows for a stall-keeper in the Market Wing — so the choice is made by seeing the action, not reading about it. The unchosen wing stays visible but dimmed, with a sign reading 'Next Festival', so the choice feels like sequencing, not losing.
fork.hypothesis: With no math evidence on record, the construct band can be probed to equal depth through either an array-first path (structure made visible as rows and columns before inverse work) or a story-first path (structure read out of contextual equal-groups language before inverse work). Both routes cover the same inverse/factor-pair demand at the same difficulty, so any performance difference isolates representational entry point rather than academic level.

activities.title: Arrival Dock: Lantern Parade Power-Up
activities.learningPurpose: Establish whether the learner can identify number of groups and group size in a story and express it as a multiplication equation, which is the base case the rest of the construct builds on.
activities.academicTarget: Given a contextual equal-groups situation with single-digit factors, state the factors, the product, and what each factor counts.
activities.mechanic: Each item is one parade scene: equal groups are drawn on screen as real festival objects (wagons of lanterns, packs of snacks, tables of chairs, trays of cups). The child answers by typing a number, tapping a matching equation, or speaking/typing a one-line explanation of what each factor counts. In the lantern problem, one factor is 8 and the other factor is 5. Explain what the 8 counts and what the 5 counts in that situation.

rubric: States that 8 counts the number of groups (wagons)
States that 5 counts the size of each group (lanterns per wagon)
Connects the two factors to the total 40 as a count of equal groups

Every correct answer sends a visible amber pulse down a conduit and lights one dock district; the parade physically advances one wagon-length toward the festival gate.
designArtifact.mathAsPower: The math IS the station's power grid: the product the child types is literally the wattage sent down the conduit. Type 40 and exactly 40 lantern-lights flicker on in a wave. A wrong count sends the wrong wattage — the lights stutter and the dock-bot's meter shows the mismatch between what was typed and what the wagons actually hold.
designArtifact.stakes: Alien families are queued outside the dark Arrival Dock in little shuttle windows, waiting. Each solved item lights a district and lets one shuttle dock; the child can see the crowd grow. The festival gate at the end of the dock only opens when all five power surges are correct.
designArtifact.consequences: A wrong answer never resets progress: the conduit sputters, the meter shows the typed number next to the true lantern count, and the scene stays live so the child can recount. Two misses on the same item make the lanterns in one group pulse in sequence (a silent skip-count cue) before the third try. The shuttle for that district simply waits — nothing is lost, but nothing lights until it's right.
designArtifact.recovery: After a miss, a small 'Recount with me' button appears (optional, never forced): tapping it makes each group glow in turn with a running subtotal (5, 10, 15...) so the child can skip-count along. The child may also drag a finger across groups to hear the running count. Answer entry stays open the entire time.
progression: Item 1: 8 wagons of 5 lanterns, fully drawn, group structure named aloud — type the total
Item 2: same scene freezes; explain what the 8 counts and what the 5 counts (type or speak one or two lines)
Item 3: snack packs at the ticket booth — groups drawn but the prompt no longer names 'groups', child locates structure alone
Item 4: face-painting tables — pick the matching equation from four floating power-cards; wrong cards fizz out harmlessly
Item 5: juice trays — sparsest scene, small thumbnails only, closest to independent work; the gate opens on success
designArtifact.worldReaction: Aliens in shuttle windows cheer and press faces to the glass when a district lights; the dock-bot's antenna spins happily on correct answers and droops sympathetically (never mockingly) on misses; conduits across the whole board map begin their gentle pulse once this node completes.
designArtifact.payoff: The festival gate irises open with a warm brass chord, the whole Arrival Dock floods amber, tiny alien families pour out of shuttles waving lantern-sticks, and the station map zooms out to show the first district glowing. A 'DOCK ONLINE' stamp thunks onto the child's engineer badge.
designArtifact.replayVariation: On replay the same five contracts run with reshuffled scene skins (wagons become hover-sleds, snacks become star-fruit) and shuffled equation-card positions; the dock-bot demo is skipped after the first completion unless requested.
designArtifact.visualDirection: Indigo dock interior with brass-and-teal trim per the board spine; every equal group is drawn as a physically countable cluster — lanterns individually visible, never abstracted to dots. Amber light is reserved exclusively for correct power. Large rounded number pad, single-line prompts in a chunky friendly typeface, read-aloud icon always present.
designArtifact.motionDirection: Slow parade drift; lantern pulses at a calm 1-per-second rhythm during counts; power surges travel conduits in about 1.5 seconds so cause-and-effect is legible. No screen shake, no rapid flashes.
designArtifact.soundDirection: Soft space-station hum underneath; each lantern lighting gives a small glass 'ting' ascending in pitch as the total fills; correct answers get a warm two-note brass swell; misses get a gentle low 'whumph' with no buzzer. All prompts have tap-to-hear narration.

howler.js for narration and ascending count tings
gsap for power-surge tweens
designArtifact.engagementPrediction: Because the first item is fully drawn and the demo shows the exact typing action, time-to-first-action should be under 20 seconds and all five items should complete in one sitting with at most one optional recount. The space-festival frame matches the child's stated space/adventure interests, so a positive first-session rating and willingness to enter the route choice is expected.
designArtifact.falsifyingEvidence: Time-to-first-action over 60 seconds or repeated demo loops would falsify the clarity claim; more than two recount-help invocations on forward items would suggest the drawn-groups scaffold isn't landing; abandonment before item 3, a skipped explanation item, or a low rating despite completion would indicate the parade framing is decoration rather than a hook and the entry should be leaner next cycle.

activities.title: Arrival Dock: The Sorting Beacon
activities.learningPurpose: Test the core misconception the page targets: treating the same two numbers as a sum or a share instead of a group-count, which is the error the multiple-choice item is designed to expose.
activities.academicTarget: Given several stories using the same pair of numbers, select the one that matches a given multiplication expression and justify why the others are not equal-groups situations.
activities.mechanic: For each item the beacon holds an expression card and three story-pods share the same number pair but different structures (equal groups, adding, sharing). The child taps a pod to feed it in. Matching pods lock in with a beam of amber light to a district; non-matching pods are gently rejected — the beacon holds them up and highlights the story words that broke the match. Two items ask for a short typed or spoken justification, entered on a simple two-tap sentence-builder plus free text.

activities.title: Arrival Dock: Fuse Check
activities.learningPurpose: Measure the prerequisite independently so that failures on structural responsibilities are not misattributed to computation, given that no fact-level evidence exists for this learner.
activities.academicTarget: Retrieve or reliably derive multiplication facts with factors 2 through 9, with accuracy and hesitation recorded separately from structural performance.
activities.mechanic: Pure, calm fact entry: one fuse at a time, bare prompt, numeric answer, untimed. Each correct product snaps the fuse alight with a satisfying click and slides the next fuse into place. There is deliberately no narrative load here — the contrast with the story-rich nodes is itself the design, honoring the contract's separation of fact fluency from structure.

designArtifact.interactionDemonstration: The panel demonstrates on a zeroth dummy fuse stamped '2 × 2': ghost-fingers type '4', the fuse clicks alight, and it retracts. Two seconds, once, skippable by touching the pad.
designArtifact.coreInteraction: Pure, calm fact entry: one fuse at a time, bare prompt, numeric answer, untimed. activities.learningPurpose: Probe the highest-demand face of the construct — treating a total as decomposable in more than one way — which distinguishes structural understanding from single-fact recall.

activities.mechanic: Freeform array construction with smart snapping: the child sets a row length by placing lanterns, then can duplicate rows with a stamp handle. A live counter shows lanterns used vs. budget (e.g., 21/24), and an equation strip auto-drafts beneath the build (e.g., '3 × 8 = ?') which the child must complete and sign. Uneven rows physically sag and spark, making 'equal rows using the whole total' a visible engineering constraint, not a rule to remember.

activities.title: Market Wing: The Stall-Keepers' Missing Numbers
activities.learningPurpose: Probe the inverse direction predicted to be weaker than forward multiplication, covering both symbolic missing-factor equations and equal-sharing contexts as the same underlying move.
activities.academicTarget: Given a total and one factor — presented either as an equation with an unknown or as an equal-rows sharing story within 48 — determine the missing factor and name the multiplication fact that verifies it.
activities.mechanic: Each stall is one item: a keeper states a short problem aloud (text mirrored, tap-to-replay), and the child answers by dialing a number into an equation socket, typing a value, or — on the capstone — assembling the missing-factor equation themselves from socket parts before solving it and naming the verifying fact. Correct sockets close the stall's circuit: lights, music, and smell-wisps all switch on at once, and the keeper begins actually selling to the crowd.
activities.engagementVariable: Whether keeping every item inside one continuous market story (narrative-first) lowers switching cost and sustains attention across the inverse band better than the grid-building entry — testing whether text is a hook or a barrier for this learner.

Equation panels are brass with satisfying socket geometry; text stays to one or two spoken-and-mirrored lines.

experience.objective: Four market stalls are wired but dark, and each keeper knows their total and one number — find each missing number and wire it in to switch a stall's whole world on.
experience.childAction: Turn the dial to 7 and press it into the empty socket of 6 × ? = 42.
experience.worldReaction: Each lit stall immediately does business — customers queue, coins clink, the keeper waves thanks whenever the child walks past; neighboring dark keepers lean out hopefully, making the next item a social pull rather than a task list.
experience.anticipation: The market's opening night is stalled: keepers wait in the dark with goods ready and alien customers drift past toward the lit districts. Every solved stall captures some of that passing crowd; four lit stalls trigger the market's grand opening.
experience.progress: Stall 1 (flags): sharing story with the equation 6 × ? = 42 pre-written — dial the missing factor → Stall 2 (lantern-oil): bare equation ? × 7 = 35 on a delivery crate — pure symbolic version of the same move → Stall 3 (badges): 48 badges, 8 per bag — the child assembles the equation from socket parts, solves it, and speaks/types the verifying fact 6 × 8 = 48 to the keeper → Stall 4 (chairs): 32 chairs, 8 per row — story leads with the total and no equation is offered, the closest to independence
experience.recovery: Optional help lives in the fiction: each keeper has a 'show me your goods' button that lays the actual objects into partial rows so the child can complete the structure by eye, and a fact-family card on every stall post flips to show the triangle of total and factors without revealing the answer. Both are one tap, never automatic.
experience.reward: The lane erupts into full market night: all four stalls trading, string-lights zig-zagging overhead, a three-piece alien band starting up, and the crowd flooding back in. The market gate to the deeper wing (ACT-STORY-02) rolls up, and one arc of Zorvax's distant ring warms.

designArtifact.title: Market Wing: The Stall-Keepers' Missing Numbers
designArtifact.openingPromise: Four market stalls are wired but dark, and each keeper knows their total and one number — find each missing number and wire it in to switch a stall's whole world on.
designArtifact.firstThreeSeconds: The camera glides into a dark night-market lane. The first stall-keeper — a moth-like alien holding a bundle of 42 flags — speaks one short line aloud with matching text: '42 flags, 6 equal rows... how many in each row?' Beside her, the equation 6 × ? = 42 hangs as a physical wiring panel with one empty socket, and a number dial is already extended toward the child.
designArtifact.firstAction: Turn the dial to 7 and press it into the empty socket of 6 × ? = 42.
designArtifact.interactionDemonstration: Before the first stall accepts input, the moth-keeper demonstrates on her own stall sign (a tiny '2 × ? = 6' name-plate): she dials 3, presses it in, and the sign lights. Three seconds, in-fiction, no tutorial text.
designArtifact.coreInteraction: Each stall is one item: a keeper states a short problem aloud (text mirrored, tap-to-replay), and the child answers by dialing a number into an equation socket, typing a value, or — on the capstone — assembling the missing-factor equation themselves from socket parts before solving it and naming the verifying fact. Correct sockets close the stall's circuit: lights, music, and smell-wisps all switch on at once, and the keeper begins actually selling to the crowd.
designArtifact.mathAsPower: The missing factor is literally the missing component in the stall's circuit. Press in the right number and power distributes visibly into exactly that structure — 6 rows of 7 flag-lights flicker on row by row, confirming the answer with the world itself. A wrong number makes the rows come out ragged on the stall's canopy, showing why it can't be right.
designArtifact.stakes: The market's opening night is stalled: keepers wait in the dark with goods ready and alien customers drift past toward the lit districts. Every solved stall captures some of that passing crowd; four lit stalls trigger the market's grand opening.
designArtifact.consequences: A wrong factor wires in and visibly fails — the canopy lights arrange into uneven rows and the keeper points at the raggedness ('That gives me rows of 8... one row's short!') before popping the number back out. The stall never breaks and the dial keeps the child's last value for adjustment. On the capstone item, a misplaced total in the equation (e.g., building 48 × 8) makes the socket physically too large for the panel — a tactile total-vs-factor cue.
designArtifact.recovery: Optional help lives in the fiction: each keeper has a 'show me your goods' button that lays the actual objects into partial rows so the child can complete the structure by eye, and a fact-family card on every stall post flips to show the triangle of total and factors without revealing the answer. Both are one tap, never automatic.
progression: Stall 1 (flags): sharing story with the equation 6 × ? = 42 pre-written — dial the missing factor
Stall 2 (lantern-oil): bare equation ? × 7 = 35 on a delivery crate — pure symbolic version of the same move
Stall 3 (badges): 48 badges, 8 per bag — the child assembles the equation from socket parts, solves it, and speaks/types the verifying fact 6 × 8 = 48 to the keeper
Stall 4 (chairs): 32 chairs, 8 per row — story leads with the total and no equation is offered, the closest to independence
designArtifact.worldReaction: Each lit stall immediately does business — customers queue, coins clink, the keeper waves thanks whenever the child walks past; neighboring dark keepers lean out hopefully, making the next item a social pull rather than a task list.
designArtifact.payoff: The lane erupts into full market night: all four stalls trading, string-lights zig-zagging overhead, a three-piece alien band starting up, and the crowd flooding back in. The market gate to the deeper wing (ACT-STORY-02) rolls up, and one arc of Zorvax's distant ring warms.
designArtifact.replayVariation: Replay re-voices keepers and re-skins goods (flags to kites, badges to star-cookies) around the frozen numbers, shuffles dial starting positions, and lets the child choose stall order after the first completion.
designArtifact.visualDirection: Dense cozy night-market palette: indigo dark broken by pools of warm stall light as progress accrues; keepers are expressive animal-adjacent aliens (moth, axolotl, pangolin, heron) with distinct silhouettes, feeding the child's animal interest without leaving the space fiction. Equation panels are brass with satisfying socket geometry; text stays to one or two spoken-and-mirrored lines.
designArtifact.motionDirection: Slow camera glides between stalls; canopy lights fill in countable rows on success; ragged-row failures animate with a gentle comic slump. Dial rotation has weighted, clicky resistance per integer.
designArtifact.soundDirection: Every keeper line is voiced with tap-to-replay; the dial clicks per number; correct sockets give a deep circuit 'chunk' followed by that stall's unique music layer joining the market mix — four stalls build a four-layer song, an audible progress bar.

planTheory.hypothesis: This learner most likely holds multiplication as a procedure attached to a fact table rather than as a structure that can be read off a situation. The page is built to break that: item 6 offers an additive and a sharing distractor for the same numbers, item 5 hides a repeated group inside a two-step story, item 7 rewards deriving 45 from a neighbor fact instead of retrieving it, and items 4 and 8 demand that one total be seen as more than one rectangle. So the diagnostic question is not "can the learner multiply within 48" but "can the learner decide what kind of multiplicative question is being asked, and move flexibly between total, factors, and array." The theory is that performance will hold on forward equal-groups items and degrade on inverse and multi-representation items (ASM-04, ASM-05), with fact recall as a confounder that must be measured separately (ASM-02) so a structural error is never misread as a computation slip. Because the entire evidence base is empty — no math accuracy, no fact bank, no prior decisions, no support observations — the smallest coherent program must sample every face of the construct once (forward equal groups, inverse/missing factor, array-to-equations, factor-pair generation, structure discrimination, derived fact) at Grade 3 depth, so a single pass separates the recall hypothesis from the structure hypothesis. Confirmation looks like clean forward work with breakdown concentrated in inverse and factor-pair items; disconfirmation looks like uniform difficulty across all six faces, which would relocate the target to fact fluency and the prerequisite band, or uniform success, which would push the construct toward multi-digit and multi-step extensions above Grade 3.
planTheory.intervention: Creator is the newly hired Festival Engineer aboard Nova Station, a space outpost where alien families are arriving for the once-a-year Starlight Festival. The station's power grid runs on equal groups: lantern racks, snack pods, badge crates, and light walls only switch on when their groups are counted and wired correctly. Every solved problem sends visible power down the station's glowing conduits, lighting up another district of the festival. The chapter opens in the Arrival Dock (three shared activities that restore basic power), then Creator chooses one of two festival wings to bring fully online — the Light Wall Wing, where power is arranged in glowing grids, or the Market Wing, where power flows through the stories of the stall-keepers. A final optional Repair Bay lets Creator fix miswired circuits other engineers got wrong. When a wing is complete, the festival launches: the whole station lights up and alien crowds pour in under a drone-lantern sky.
